title: 2D/3D Computer Graphics (Intro & Systems)

concepts.name: Definition
concepts.description: Computer Graphics (CG) is the study of generating and manipulating images and animations via computers.

concepts.name: Main Tasks
concepts.description: Modeling (describe geometry), Rendering (generate 2D image from 3D), Animation (change over time).

concepts.name: Applications
concepts.description: Games, simulations, CAD/CAM, medical imaging, virtual training, user interfaces, etc.

concepts.name: Graphics Pipeline
concepts.description: Comprises stages like modeling, transformation, lighting, rasterization, and display. (CG pipeline processes geometry → pixels.)

concepts.name: Graphics System Components
concepts.description: Host CPU, GPU/graphics processor, large RAM, frame buffer (memory for pixel data), and display device (CRT/LCD).

concepts.name: Display Hardware
concepts.description: Raster-scan displays update rows of pixels; resolution and refresh rate matter. (E.g. frame buffer stores pixel RGB values.)

concepts.name: Coordinate Systems
concepts.description: Objects defined in world coordinates; transformed to device coordinates (via viewport mapping) for display.

concepts.name: Color Model
concepts.description: A mathematical scheme to represent colors as tuples (e.g. RGB triple). (Color space is specific values interpreted with viewing conditions.)

concepts.name: RGB (Additive)
concepts.description: Based on mixing Red, Green, Blue light. Used for displays. (0,0,0=black; 1,1,1 or

concepts.name: CMY(K) (Subtractive)
concepts.description: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow (and often Black for printers). Relation: C=1–R, M=1–G,

concepts.name: Concept
concepts.description: Y=1–B. CMYK used in printing (K = black for efficiency). Undercolor removal in CMYK subtracts CMY components to add pure black ink, saving color ink.

concepts.name: HSV/HSL
concepts.description: Hue (color type, angle 0–360°), Saturation (intensity of color), Value/Lightness (brightness).

concepts.name: Concept
concepts.description: Useful for color selection.

concepts.name: YIQ/YUV
concepts.description: Luma-chroma models (used in TV); Y = brightness, I/Q or U/V = color differences. (Often used for compression; not heavily tested unless slides covered them.)

concepts.name: RGB Cube
concepts.description: Colors form a cube in RGB space. Diagonal from (0,0,0) to (1,1,1) goes from black to white with gray shades.

concepts.name: Gamma Correction (Trap)
concepts.description: Real displays do not respond linearly to voltage. In many problems, assume gamma = 1 (ignored) unless stated. (The slide warns “gamma correction usually ignored.”)

concepts.name: Indexed Color & LUT
concepts.description: An image can use an 8-bit index into a 256-color palette (LUT). To convert 24- bit (true color) to 8-bit, quantize each channel (e.g. 3 bits R, 3 G, 2 B) and compute palette index. E.g., index = (r_index8 + g_index)4 + b_index.

high_yield_notes: Gamma Caveat: Always clarify if gamma correction is applied. Many solutions on exams assume no gamma (linear). The slide explicitly warns that gamma is usually ignored – an exam trap.

questions.question: Define computer graphics and list its three main tasks.
questions.answer: CG is the creation/manipulation of visual images and animations via computers . Main tasks are Modeling (geometry), Rendering (image generation), and Animation (time-variation).
questions.explanation: The definition and tasks are core (per slides and sources). Model geometry → Render to pixels → Animate changes over time.

questions.question: What are typical components of a graphics system, and what is the role of the frame buffer?
questions.answer: A graphics system includes a CPU/GPU, memory, and a frame buffer connected to a display. The frame buffer is a block of RAM holding pixel color values for the screen.
questions.explanation: The frame buffer stores the image that gets sent to the display. High resolution or color depth means a larger frame buffer (more memory needed).

questions.question: Compare vector graphics and raster graphics.
questions.answer: Vector graphics store geometry (points, lines) mathematically and scale without quality loss; Raster graphics store pixels in a grid. Vector-to-display requires rasterization, while rasters have fixed resolution.
questions.explanation: This tests understanding of how images are represented and why rasterization is needed.

questions.question: Why might one use lower color depth or resolution?
questions.answer: To reduce memory usage and increase processing speed at the cost of image quality. It trades off detail (fewer bits or pixels) for performance or storage.
questions.explanation: This links to “trade image quality for speed” (slide outcome). Common exam trap is forgetting the performance benefit of quantization.

questions.question: Name one example of a real-time CG application and one offline CG application.
questions.answer: Real-time example: video game graphics. Offline example: CGI in movies or visual effects.
questions.explanation: Show difference – games run on the fly, film rendering can take hours per frame.

high_yield_notes: Gamma Caveat: Always clarify if gamma correction is applied. Many solutions on exams assume no gamma (linear). The slide explicitly warns that gamma is usually ignored – an exam trap.
Color Model Distinctions: Don’t confuse HSV vs HSL; Hue is the same, but HSL’s L (lightness) is different from HSV’s V. Some instructors expect noting that HSL = 0 saturation still yields grayscale.
RGB vs CMY Relations: A common mistake is mixing them up; remember CMY subtracts light, so white (all light) is (0,0,0) in RGB, but (0,0,0) in CMY yields white too (if defined as 1–RGB).
Undercolor Removal: Adding K in printers avoids muddy colors. If asked, note CMYK allows using less ink.
Quantization: When computing LUT index, remember to floor or use integer division. Errors often happen by off-by-one in slice calculation.

questions.question: What is the difference between additive and subtractive color models? Give an example of each.
questions.answer: Additive (e.g. RGB) mixes light; adding R, G, B yields white light. Subtractive (e.g. CMY) mixes pigments or filters; mixing C, M, Y gives black (ideally).
questions.explanation: RGB for screens, CMY for printing. Additive starts at black (no light), subtractive starts at white (paper).

questions.question: How does histogram equalization improve image contrast? Write the basic transformation formula.
questions.answer: It remaps pixel intensities using the CDF of the image so that output intensities are spread across [0, L–1]. The transform is $T(i) = \mathrm{CDF}(i)$ (normalized).
questions.explanation: The CDF-based mapping makes output histogram uniform. Key formula: new intensity = cumulative probability up to old intensity.

questions.question: Convert 24-bit RGB (R=20, G=33, B=150) to an 8-bit indexed color using 3-3-2 bits per channel. Show steps.
questions.answer: Divide 0–255 into 8 slices for R,G, 4 slices for B. R-index = ⌊20/32⌋ = 0; G-index = ⌊33/32⌋ = 1; B- index = ⌊150/64⌋ = 2. Then index = (08 + 1)4 + 2 = 6.
questions.explanation: Each 24-bit color channel is quantized. The formula is (R_slice * 8 + G_slice)*4 + B_slice for 3-3-2 bits.

questions.question: What is the RGB value of pure yellow? In CMY terms, what would that be?
questions.answer: Yellow = (255,255,0) in RGB. In CMY, that’s C=0, M=0, Y=1 (or 0% cyan, 0% magenta, 100% yellow) because Y = 1–B = 1.
questions.explanation: Yellow light is red+green. In CMY, B=0 → Y=1; R=1→C=0, G=1→M=0.

questions.question: Give one advantage of the HSV model over RGB for user color selection.
questions.answer: HSV separates color (hue) from intensity (value), so users can pick a hue and then adjust saturation/brightness. It’s more intuitive (turn “color wheel” for hue).
questions.explanation: In RGB, hue and brightness are entangled across three numbers, but HSV’s H,S,V correspond more to human color concepts.

concepts.name: Order Matters
concepts.description: Transformations are non-commutative. E.g. rotating then translating ≠ translating then rotating (unless center is origin). Always apply matrix operations in correct sequence.

concepts.name: Pixels vs Coordinates
concepts.description: Logical coordinates (real numbers) map to pixel grid. To draw a point at (x,y), usually round or floor to nearest integer pixel (floor gives largest integer ≤ coordinate).

concepts.name: DDA Line Algorithm
concepts.description: Incremental method. Given endpoints P1(x1,y1), P2(x2,y2), compute steps = max(Δx,Δy). Increment x and y by small amounts each step. Formula uses floating arithmetic.

concepts.name: Bresenham’s Line Algorithm
concepts.description: Integer-based. Uses a decision parameter to choose whether to increment y (for gentle slopes). More efficient than DDA (uses only addition, no floating). Common pseudocode initializes error = 2Δy–Δx, etc.

concepts.name: Slope Cases
concepts.description: For slopes >1 or negative slopes, reflect or swap axes. In practice, ensure walking in the dominant direction (steep vs shallow) to keep one axis as independent.

concepts.name: Endpoint Handling
concepts.description: Typically plot both endpoints. Many implementations ensure P1 and P2 are both drawn.

concepts.name: Aliasing
concepts.description: Raster lines show stair-step “jaggies”. Antialiasing reduces this but usually not covered in basic CG.

high_yield_notes: Comparisons: DDA easier conceptually but slower (float mults). Bresenham is faster (only integer add/sub) – exam may ask which is more efficient.
Common Pitfall: Forgetting to initialize error correctly or increment y at right times. Many students get off-by-one errors.
Continuity: Must handle all octants: usually take absolute values of slope and step accordingly.

questions.question: Write the 2D rotation matrix for angle θ and use it to compute the image of point (1,0) when θ=90°.
questions.answer:
The 2D rotation matrix is:
R(θ) = [[cos θ, -sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]]

For θ = 90°:
cos 90° = 0, sin 90° = 1
R(90°) = [[0, -1], [1, 0]]

Applying to point (1, 0):
x' = 1 * cos 90° - 0 * sin 90° = 0
y' = 1 * sin 90° + 0 * cos 90° = 1
Thus, the rotated point is (0, 1).
questions.explanation: Cos(90°)=0, sin(90°)=1. The matrix sends (1,0) to (0,1), a 90° CCW rotation. x = ′ x + t , y = x ′ y + t . y • x = ′ S x, y = x ′ S y. y • = (x′ y′) . (cos θ sin θ −sin θ cos θ ) (x y) • • • • • • 1 0 0 0 1 0 tx ty 1

questions.question: How would you reflect the point (3,5) across the line y=x?
questions.answer: Swap coordinates: (x',y') = (5,3).
questions.explanation: Reflection in y=x just swaps x and y. A trap is mixing up axes – memorize swap.

questions.question: Given point (2,3), apply shear with Shx=1 (x-shear), then translation (tx=1, ty=–2). What is the final point?
questions.explanation: * Order is shear then translate. Check each step carefully.

questions.question: What happens if you apply scaling by (–1,1)?
questions.answer: x' = –1·x, y' = 1·y. This reflects the object across the y-axis (and scales by 1).
questions.explanation: Negative scale flips direction. A scale of (–1,1) is equivalent to reflecting in y-axis.

questions.question: Why do we use homogeneous coordinates for 2D transforms? Give one advantage.
questions.answer: It allows representing translation as matrix multiplication (by adding a 3rd coordinate 1). This unifies all transforms (translation, rotation, scale, etc.) as matrix multiplications.
questions.explanation: Without homogeneous coords, translation isn’t linear. Homogeneous makes combining transforms straightforward (just multiply 3×3 matrices).

title: Rasterization (Scan Conversion)

concepts.name: Pixels vs Coordinates
concepts.description: Logical coordinates (real numbers) map to pixel grid. To draw a point at (x,y), usually round or floor to nearest integer pixel (floor gives largest integer ≤ coordinate).

concepts.name: DDA Line Algorithm
concepts.description: Incremental method. Given endpoints P1(x1,y1), P2(x2,y2), compute steps = max(Δx,Δy). Increment x and y by small amounts each step. Formula uses floating arithmetic.

concepts.name: Bresenham’s Line Algorithm
concepts.description: Integer-based. Uses a decision parameter to choose whether to increment y (for gentle slopes). More efficient than DDA (uses only addition, no floating). Common pseudocode initializes error = 2Δy–Δx, etc.

concepts.name: Slope Cases
concepts.description: For slopes >1 or negative slopes, reflect or swap axes. In practice, ensure walking in the dominant direction (steep vs shallow) to keep one axis as independent.

concepts.name: Endpoint Handling
concepts.description: Typically plot both endpoints. Many implementations ensure P1 and P2 are both drawn.

concepts.name: Aliasing
concepts.description: Raster lines show stair-step “jaggies”. Antialiasing reduces this but usually not covered in basic CG.

concepts.name: Circle Definition
concepts.description: $x^2 + y^2 = r^2$. Only need compute 1/8th of circle (from 0° to 45°) and mirror to other octants.

concepts.name: Midpoint Circle Algorithm
concepts.description: Similar to Bresenham line. Starts at (0,r). Uses decision variable $p = 1- r$; iterate x from 0 to y, update p: if p<0, choose E pixel (x+1,y); else choose SE pixel (x+1,y-1) and update p with different increments. Plot symmetry points.

concepts.name: 8-way Symmetry
concepts.description: From computed (x,y), plot points (±x,±y) and (±y,±x). (Total 8 per octant).

concepts.name: Ellipse Algorithm (if any)
concepts.description: Midpoint ellipse analog splits into two regions (slope 1 boundary). (Often not tested unless lecture explicitly taught.)

concepts.name: Parameters
concepts.description: Only need integer radius. If center ≠ origin, translate after computation.

high_yield_notes: First Octant: Compute until x=y (45°) or decision changes. After that, swap roles of x and y.
Decisions: The initial p = 1–r, update rules p_new = p + 2x + 3 (when E) or p + 2(x–y) + 5 (when SE).
Off-by-one in these formulas is a common exam pitfall.
Symmetry: Always mirror the points. Often students forget to plot all 8 symmetrical points.
Comparison: Like lines, uses only adds (no multiplications) and integer operations – it’s efficient.
Trap: Remember to plot at least one point per octant; the trivial (r,0) and (0,r) points.

questions.question: Compare DDA and Bresenham line algorithms in terms of arithmetic operations.
questions.answer: DDA uses floating-point increments (multiplication/addition each step). Bresenham uses only integer addition/subtraction (decision variable), making it faster and more efficient.
questions.explanation: Bresenham’s algorithm avoids costly floats. On older hardware, Bresenham was preferred for speed.

questions.question: Using Bresenham’s algorithm, what decision would you make at the midpoint for a line from (0,0) to (5,3)? (Outline steps.)
questions.answer: Δx=5, Δy=3, initial p = 2Δy–Δx = 23–5 = 1. Steps: at x=0->1 (p=1>=0) → y=1, new p = p + 2(Δy–Δx) = 1+2(3–5) = -3. Next, p<0 → (x2,y1), update p = -3+2Δy=3. Continue similarly. The sequence of chosen pixels approximates the line.
questions.explanation: * Illustrates decision variable updates. For brevity, the key is showing update logic.

questions.question: Why does Bresenham’s algorithm produce a straight line without gaps?
questions.answer: It always steps one pixel in x (and sometimes in y), ensuring continuous adjacency. The decision param ensures the best approximation to the true line each step.
questions.explanation: Unlike simply rounding, Bresenham’s logic keeps one pixel gap-free.

questions.question: How is a single point drawn in raster coordinates?
questions.answer: Take the real (x,y) coordinates and use a rounding or floor method to choose the nearest pixel (e.g., Pixel(floor(x), floor(y))).
questions.explanation: In practice we map float to int. The slide suggests Floor method (largest integer ≤ coord).

questions.question: For a line with negative slope, how do line-drawing algorithms handle it?
questions.answer: Reflect or swap endpoints so slope is positive, draw the line, then reflect back. For Bresenham, one can increment y downward when needed (treat Δy as absolute and adjust sign).
questions.explanation: Algorithms are usually described for slope 0–1; handling other octants requires symmetry or sign adjustment.

questions.question: Why do we only calculate 1/8th of a circle when using midpoint algorithms?
questions.answer: Because of 8-way symmetry. Computing one octant and reflecting yields the full circle, greatly reducing work (by factor 8).
questions.explanation: For each (x,y) in one octant, the other points (±x,±y, ±y,±x) are placed.

questions.question: What is the initial decision parameter $p$ for the midpoint circle algorithm of radius r?
questions.explanation: Standard derivation (see textbooks). The first step uses this to choose pixel at (1,r) or (1,r–1).

questions.question: If at a given step $p<0$, which pixel do you choose and how do you update $p$?
questions.answer: If $p<0$, the next pixel is East: $(x+1, y)$ and update $p = p + 2x + 3$.
questions.explanation: This maintains $p$ = difference from true circle. The formula comes from evaluating $p + 2x + 3$.

questions.question: How is ellipsis drawing different from circles? (Conceptual)
questions.answer: An ellipse has two radii (rx, ry) and lower symmetry (4-way). The midpoint ellipse algorithm handles two regions (dx>dy vs dx<dy) separately. It uses different decision criteria because $x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1$ is not rotationally invariant like a circle.
questions.explanation: Unless needed, mention main difference: shape formula and 4-way symmetry.

questions.question: What is a common advantage of midpoint-based drawing algorithms?
questions.answer: They use only integer arithmetic (efficient) and ensure continuity. Also, by using symmetry they reduce computations.
questions.explanation: Contrast with naive approaches (like computing y via sqrt) which would be slow.

title: Region Filling

concepts.name: Boundary Fill
concepts.description: Start from an interior seed point and expand until a boundary color is reached.

concepts.name: Typically recursive
concepts.description: at pixel (x,y), if its color ≠ boundary and ≠ fill color, set to fill color and recurse on neighbors.

concepts.name: Flood Fill
concepts.description: Similar but stops on a specified original color instead of a boundary color. (Flood fill fills all connected pixels of an original color.)

concepts.name: Connectivity
concepts.description: 4-connected (up, down, left, right) or 8-connected (diagonals included). E.g. 4- connected has 4 neighbors, 8-connected has 8 neighbors.

concepts.name: Use Cases
concepts.description: Fill closed shapes (like coloring in a polygon).

high_yield_notes: Recursion Pitfall: Naïve boundary/flood fill can cause stack overflow if region is large. (Non- recursive methods or scan-line fills avoid this.)
Seed Selection: Must start inside region; if outside boundary color polygon, nothing happens.
Boundary vs Flood: Boundary-fill requires a clear boundary color; flood-fill requires a known original color.
Exam Trap: Don’t confuse with clipping. Fill colors inside region only. Check connectivity definition in question (4 vs 8 connectivity changes result).
Implementation: Ensure base case checks both boundary and already filled colors to avoid infinite loops.

questions.question: What’s the difference between boundary fill and flood fill algorithms?
questions.answer: Boundary-fill stops at boundary color; it fills until it reaches a boundary color. Flood-fill stops when it hits the original color it’s replacing. In other words, boundary-fill uses a boundary value, flood-fill uses the initial region color as the stopping condition.
questions.explanation: If filling a region until edge, boundary-fill is used. If filling by color match, flood-fill.

questions.question: Why might a flood-fill algorithm fill an unintended area?
questions.answer: If the starting seed color is shared with other regions (not isolated), flood-fill will spread through all connected same-color areas. If boundary not properly enclosed, fill leaks.
questions.explanation: Make sure boundaries or segmentation isolate areas, or choose correct seed.

questions.question: How can using 8-connected neighbors instead of 4-connected affect fill?
questions.answer: 8-connected includes diagonals, so more pixels get filled (diagonal adjacency allows “leakage”). Using 4-connected may leave diagonal holes in a diagonally connected region.
questions.explanation: 8-connectivity yields a “solid” fill; 4-connectivity can leave corner gaps.

questions.question: Outline a pseudocode snippet for boundary-fill with 4 neighbors.
questions.explanation: Recursively fills the 4-connected neighboring pixels (up, down, left, right) until a pixel with the boundary color or already-filled color is encountered.

title: Image Enhancement (Spatial Domain)

concepts.name: Histogram of an Image
concepts.description: Graph of frequency of each intensity level.

concepts.name: Contrast Stretch (Linear)
concepts.description: Scale pixel values so the darkest becomes 0 and brightest becomes 255.

concepts.name: Histogram Equalization
concepts.description: Spread intensities to flatten histogram. Compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of pixel values, then map each pixel to its CDF value scaled. Result: more uniform histogram. Key idea: $T(i) = \mathrm{CDF}(i)$ (normalized)【19†L273-

concepts.name: Gamma Correction
concepts.description: Adjust brightness nonlinearly: new = old^γ (or inverse). Useful for correcting display gamma or brightening/darkening images. (E.g., γ<1 brightens dark images.)

concepts.name: Frequency Domain
concepts.description: Represent image with Fourier transform. Low frequencies = smooth variations; high frequencies = edges/detail.

concepts.name: Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)
concepts.description: Converts 2D image to frequency components. (No need formula on exam, just concept.)

concepts.name: Filtering
concepts.description: In freq domain, low-pass filtering removes high frequencies (blur/smooth), high-pass filters remove low frequencies (sharpen/enhance edges).

concepts.name: Convolution Theorem
concepts.description: Spatial convolution = multiplication in freq domain. Often faster for large kernels with FFT.

concepts.name: Filter Examples
concepts.description: Ideal low-pass (circular cutoff), Gaussian low-pass, Butterworth, etc. Ideal often causes ringing (Gibbs phenomenon).

high_yield_notes: Darkest/Brightest Pixels: Contrast stretch requires finding I_min, I_max (often by scanning histogram endpoints). If a few pixels are extreme (outliers), stretching can oversaturate.
Histogram Equalization Trap: It maximizes contrast globally but can produce weird effects (e.g., amplify noise). It’s not local adaptive enhancement.
Color Images: Usually apply equalization to intensity (grayscale or luminance), not per RGB channel, to avoid color shifts (unless instructed otherwise).
Gamma Usage: If device has gamma ≠1, sometimes first linearize by gamma-1, do processing, then re-apply gamma. Exams might assume gamma=1 (no correction needed).
Sampled Data CDF: Use normalized CDF (range 0–1) then scale to [0,L–1]. Rounding at end.

questions.question: A 3-bit grayscale image has intensity values {0,1,2,...,7}. If a pixel value 2 occurs 5 times, 4 occurs 10 times, and 6 occurs 5 times (total 20 pixels), what is the equalized value of intensity 4?
questions.explanation: * Equalization maps 4 to 5. Shows using CDF formula.

questions.question: What effect does a 3x3 mean filter have on an image?
questions.answer: It replaces each pixel with the average of its 3×3 neighborhood, smoothing (blurring) the image and reducing random noise, but it also blurs edges.
questions.explanation: Mean filter is linear low-pass. It reduces variance (noise) but also reduces detail.

questions.question: Why is a median filter preferred for salt-and-pepper noise?
questions.answer: Because median preserves edges better and effectively removes isolated extreme pixels. Replacing center with median kills outliers without blurring edges as much as averaging.
questions.explanation: Median is non-linear and robust to impulse noise.

questions.question: Explain unsharp masking in image sharpening.
questions.answer: Compute a blurred version of the image, subtract from original to get high-frequency (edges), then add back to original. Formula: I_new = I_orig + k(I_orig – I_blur). Equivalently, use a Laplacian filter.
questions.explanation: * It’s called “unsharp” because you subtract a smoothed (unsharp) image to emphasize edges.

questions.question: What does applying a high-pass filter to an image do? Give an example of a high-pass mask.
questions.answer: It enhances edges by removing low-frequency content. Example Laplacian mask: [[0,-1,0],[-1,4,-1], [0,-1,0]] highlights regions where pixel differs from neighbors.
questions.explanation: High-pass allows fine details, edges; reduces smooth areas. Laplacian is common.

title: Image Processing (Frequency Domain)

concepts.name: Frequency Domain
concepts.description: Represent image with Fourier transform. Low frequencies = smooth variations; high frequencies = edges/detail.

concepts.name: Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT)
concepts.description: Converts 2D image to frequency components. (No need formula on exam, just concept.)

concepts.name: Filtering
concepts.description: In freq domain, low-pass filtering removes high frequencies (blur/smooth), high-pass filters remove low frequencies (sharpen/enhance edges).

concepts.name: Convolution Theorem
concepts.description: Spatial convolution = multiplication in freq domain. Often faster for large kernels with FFT.

concepts.name: Filter Examples
concepts.description: Ideal low-pass (circular cutoff), Gaussian low-pass, Butterworth, etc. Ideal often causes ringing (Gibbs phenomenon).

concepts.name: Spatial vs Frequency
concepts.description: Some tasks (e.g., blurring) can be done in either domain. Multi-step: transform, multiply by mask, inverse transform.

high_yield_notes: Space vs Frequency Complexity: For large kernels, FFT can be more efficient (O(N log N) vs O(Nk^2)). The midterm has a question hinting “FFT more efficient for large kernels” (likely high confidence concept).
Edge Effects: Frequency domain filtering assumes periodic extension; check image padding/ truncation issues.

Traps: Don’t confuse high-pass with “removes edges” – actually it emphasizes edges. (See exam misconceptions in Lecture 8 Q’s: “High-pass filtering removes edges” is false – it removes low frequencies, preserving edges.)
Sharpening in Frequency: Adding a high-pass result to original image (like unsharp mask) yields enhancement.

questions.question: A 3-bit grayscale image has intensity values {0,1,2,...,7}. If a pixel value 2 occurs 5 times, 4 occurs 10 times, and 6 occurs 5 times (total 20 pixels), what is the equalized value of intensity 4?
questions.explanation: * Equalization maps 4 to 5. Shows using CDF formula.

questions.question: What effect does a 3x3 mean filter have on an image?
questions.answer: It replaces each pixel with the average of its 3×3 neighborhood, smoothing (blurring) the image and reducing random noise, but it also blurs edges.
questions.explanation: Mean filter is linear low-pass. It reduces variance (noise) but also reduces detail.

questions.question: Why is a median filter preferred for salt-and-pepper noise?
questions.answer: Because median preserves edges better and effectively removes isolated extreme pixels. Replacing center with median kills outliers without blurring edges as much as averaging.
questions.explanation: Median is non-linear and robust to impulse noise.

questions.question: Explain unsharp masking in image sharpening.
questions.answer: Compute a blurred version of the image, subtract from original to get high-frequency (edges), then add back to original. Formula: I_new = I_orig + k(I_orig – I_blur). Equivalently, use a Laplacian filter.
questions.explanation: * It’s called “unsharp” because you subtract a smoothed (unsharp) image to emphasize edges.

questions.question: What does applying a high-pass filter to an image do? Give an example of a high-pass mask.
questions.answer: It enhances edges by removing low-frequency content. Example Laplacian mask: [[0,-1,0],[-1,4,-1], [0,-1,0]] highlights regions where pixel differs from neighbors.
questions.explanation: High-pass allows fine details, edges; reduces smooth areas. Laplacian is common.

questions.question: Describe what a 2D Gaussian low-pass filter does to an image and why it’s separable.
questions.answer: It smooths (blurs) the image by averaging pixel values with a Gaussian-weighted kernel, preserving edges less than an ideal filter. Separable because a 2D Gaussian = row-wise 1D Gaussian followed by column-wise 1D Gaussian.
questions.explanation: Separable means convolution can be done in two passes (rows then columns), speeding computation.

questions.question: A filter has frequency response that is 1 for |f|<f_c and 0 otherwise. What is this filter and what artifact can it introduce?
questions.answer: Ideal low-pass filter (circular cutoff). It can introduce ringing artifacts (Gibbs effect) near sharp edges in spatial domain.
questions.explanation: The abrupt cutoff in freq causes oscillations in space.

questions.question: Why might one use the frequency domain to apply a large filter instead of doing it directly in the spatial domain?
questions.answer: Because convolution with large kernels is faster via FFTs (O(N log N) operations) than direct convolution (O(N k^2)). Large 2D kernels are impractical to implement by direct summation.
questions.explanation: Efficiency trade-off: overhead of FFT but gains for large sizes.

questions.question: In the context of image smoothing, what is the difference between a box filter and a Gaussian filter?
questions.answer: A box (mean) filter assigns equal weight to neighbors; a Gaussian gives more weight to nearer pixels. Gaussian causes less blockiness and better preserves central intensity.
questions.explanation: Gaussian is smoother in frequency (no sharp cutoff).

questions.question: What is the effect of multiplying an image by −1 before displaying it (in frequency domain)?
questions.answer: Multiplying by (−1)^(x+y) (sometimes done to center freq) shifts the zero-frequency to center. This is standard practice but exam likely won't ask this detail.
questions.explanation: Not crucial, skip if not needed.

title: Augmented & Virtual/Mixed Reality

concepts.name: Augmented Reality (AR)
concepts.description: Overlays computer-generated content onto the real environment

concepts.name: Concept
concepts.description: . It enhances reality by adding virtual objects in real-time. (e.g. Pokemon Go on a camera view.)

concepts.name: VR vs AR
concepts.description: VR is a fully virtual environment, replacing reality. AR uses the real world as base. (AR adds to real; VR immerses in all virtual.)

concepts.name: Marker-based
concepts.description: Recognizes a printed marker (e.g. ARToolkit) to place 3D model.

concepts.name: Markerless/Location-based
concepts.description: Uses GPS/SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) to align 3D content with real world (no pre-defined markers).

concepts.name: Projection-based
concepts.description: Projects images onto real surfaces.

concepts.name: Non-immersive
concepts.description: Desktop 3D simulation (not full immersion, e.g. PC driving sim).

concepts.name: Semi-immersive
concepts.description: Big screens or partial VR (like flight simulators with a cockpit).

concepts.name: Fully immersive
concepts.description: HMDs (head-mounted displays) or VR caves.

concepts.name: Mixed Reality (MR/XR)
concepts.description: A continuum blending real and virtual. MR usually means digital objects anchored to real world and able to interact with it. XR (Extended Reality) is an umbrella for

concepts.name: Concept
concepts.description: AR+VR+MR.

concepts.name: 360° Video
concepts.description: Full spherical video capturing all angles. When viewed on HMD, user can look around.

concepts.name: Concept
concepts.description: It’s not interactive (camera motion only), but provides an immersive scene.

concepts.name: Pipeline
concepts.description: Steps often: Acquire image → Preprocess (noise reduction) → Feature Extraction (edges, corners, textures) → Recognition/Classification/Detection → Decision (class label, object identity, etc.).

concepts.name: Classification
concepts.description: Identify main object (one label for whole image). E.g. “This is a cat.”

concepts.name: Object Detection
concepts.description: Find and classify objects with bounding boxes. E.g. “Person at (x,y), Car at (u,v).”

concepts.name: Edge Detection

high_yield_notes: Data Difference: CG creates synthetic data; CV deals with noisy real data (lighting, occlusions).
Emphasize that.
Feature vs Template: Early CV used hand-crafted features; modern CV (not likely covered) uses ML/ AI. But exam likely sticks to basics (edges, thresholds).

questions.question: Define Augmented Reality and give one example of its use.
questions.answer: AR overlays computer-generated images or info onto the real world in real-time. Example: Smartphones showing virtual furniture in a room (e.g. IKEA Place app).
questions.explanation: It’s interactive and contextual. AR enables enhancing real scenes, unlike VR.

questions.question: What is SLAM and why is it important in AR?
questions.answer: SLAM = Simultaneous Localization and Mapping. It builds a map of unknown environment while tracking device location. In AR, it allows markerless tracking (the device understands its position • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • • 1. 2. 12 relative to environment) without pre-set markers.
questions.explanation: Markerless AR and HoloLens use SLAM to place objects stably in real world.

questions.question: Describe one difference between Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality.
questions.answer: VR immerses the user in a fully digital environment (blocks real world), while AR keeps the real world and overlays additional info.
questions.explanation: Key difference: AR augments reality, VR replaces it. This is often tested.

questions.question: What are the three levels of VR immersion?
questions.answer: Non-immersive (desktop 3D, e.g. computer game), semi-immersive (CAVE or wide-screen simulators), fully immersive (HMD or dome with head tracking).
questions.explanation: This taxonomy comes from slides (though exact terms may vary).

questions.question: What is a 360° video and how does it relate to VR?
questions.answer: A 360° video is a spherical video that captures all directions. When viewed on VR goggles, you can look around in the fixed viewpoint (the camera can’t move). It’s a passive VR experience (no motion inside scene).
questions.explanation: It’s like watching a pre-recorded real scene from all angles.

concepts.name: Definition
concepts.description: Computer Vision (CV) is about interpreting images and videos – enabling computers to

concepts.name: Concept

concepts.name: Pipeline

concepts.name: Classification

concepts.name: Object Detection
concepts.description: Find and classify objects with bounding boxes. E.g. “Person at (x,y), Car at (u,v).”

concepts.name: Segmentation
concepts.description: Label each pixel (e.g. background vs object; semantic segmentation or instance segmentation).

concepts.name: Edge Detection
concepts.description: Find pixel-level edges (Sobel, Canny). Preliminary step for many tasks.

concepts.name: Thresholding

concepts.name: Edge Detection (Example)

concepts.name: Segmentation

high_yield_notes: Data Difference: CG creates synthetic data; CV deals with noisy real data (lighting, occlusions).
Emphasize that.
Feature vs Template: Early CV used hand-crafted features; modern CV (not likely covered) uses ML/ AI. But exam likely sticks to basics (edges, thresholds).
Common Trap: Don’t mix “detection” with “segmentation.” Detection boxes vs pixel classification.
Example Application: Brain tumor detection via threshold (slides gave that example). They might ask to describe steps: e.g. “Threshold MRI to segment tumor vs background.”
Multiple Objects: Classification handles one object per image; detection can handle many; segmentation yields precise shape.

questions.question: What is the main goal of computer vision? How is it different from image processing?
questions.answer: CV’s goal is to extract meaningful information from images (interpret content). Image Processing mainly modifies images (improve quality, transform). CV analyzes, IP enhances.
questions.explanation: Distinguish generation/enhancement vs analysis. Example: IP might denoise; CV might detect a tumor in the denoised image.

questions.question: A system labels an image as “cat” or “dog.” Is this classification, detection, or segmentation?
questions.answer: Classification (assign one label to the whole image).
questions.explanation: There’s no localization or per-pixel mask, just global label.

questions.question: How does object detection differ from semantic segmentation?
questions.answer: Object detection finds objects and draws bounding boxes. Semantic segmentation labels every pixel with a class. Detection gives coarse location; segmentation gives exact shape.
questions.explanation: Key difference: segmentation is pixel-level classification.

questions.question: Explain the role of thresholding in CV, with an example.
questions.answer: Thresholding converts a grayscale image to binary by choosing a cutoff (T). E.g. to detect bright objects, set pixels > T = object (1), else background (0). Example: simple tumor detection on MRI.
questions.explanation: Simple but effective if object is much brighter/darker.

questions.question: What is an edge detector (e.g. Sobel or Canny) used for?
questions.answer: To find significant intensity changes (edges) in an image. Edges often correspond to object boundaries or features.
questions.explanation: Preprocessing step, often feeding into higher-level tasks (like segmentation or recognition).
